questions.q: What is the key difference between PyTorch's eager mode and torch.compile?
options: Eager mode only works on CPU; torch.compile only works on GPU
Eager mode executes each operation immediately as Python calls it; torch.compile traces operations into a graph that can be optimized and fused
torch.compile requires rewriting the model in a different language
There is no functional difference — torch.compile is purely cosmetic
questions.explain: Eager mode runs one op at a time with no visibility into what comes next. torch.compile traces the model's operations into a graph, which its backend (TorchInductor) can then optimize and fuse.

questions.q: Why is the very first call to a torch.compile-wrapped model noticeably slower than a normal eager forward pass?
options: PyTorch loads the entire dataset into memory on the first call
PyTorch traces and compiles the graph on that first call; later calls reuse the compiled artifact
The GPU driver must be reinstalled on first use
torch.compile always runs twice as slow as eager mode, permanently
questions.explain: Compilation happens lazily on first invocation. That one-time tracing and compiling cost is paid up front; subsequent calls reuse the already-compiled graph and run fast.

questions.q: Which torch.compile mode spends the most time compiling in exchange for searching for the fastest possible kernels?
options: "default"
"reduce-overhead"
"max-autotune"
"eager"
questions.explain: "max-autotune" trades a much longer compile time for the fastest kernels it can find, generally worthwhile only for long-running training jobs where that cost gets amortized.

questions.q: What backend does torch.compile use by default to generate optimized kernels?
options: TorchScript
ONNX Runtime
TorchInductor
cuDNN alone, with no additional compiler
questions.explain: TorchInductor is torch.compile's default backend compiler — it takes the traced graph and generates optimized, often-fused kernels from it.

questions.q: What is a "graph break," and when is it most likely to occur?
options: A hardware failure that halts training entirely
A point where torch.compile falls back to eager execution for a portion of the model, often due to Python control flow that depends on tensor values rather than shapes
An error thrown when a model has too many layers to compile
The moment torch.compile finishes compiling and switches to fast mode
questions.explain: A graph break happens when torch.compile can't trace through a section of code cleanly — commonly data-dependent control flow — so it falls back to eager mode for that part. The model still runs correctly, just without the speedup there.
